crossref.title: Evolving to a New Dominant Logic for Marketing
crossref.abstract: <jats:p> Marketing inherited a model of exchange from economics, which had a dominant logic based on the exchange of “goods,” which usually are manufactured output. The dominant logic focused on tangible resources, embedded value, and transactions. Over the past several decades, new perspectives have emerged that have a revised logic focused on intangible resources, the cocreation of value, and relationships. The authors believe that the new perspectives are converging to form a new dominant logic for marketing, one in which service provision rather than goods is fundamental to economic exchange. The authors explore this evolving logic and the corresponding shift in perspective for marketing scholars, marketing practitioners, and marketing educators. </jats:p>

citations.title: Building Resident Loyalty through Tribe Marketing: The Mediating Roles of Customer Engagement and Value Co-Creation in Housing Communities
contexts: From a theoretical standpoint, the positive association between co-creation and loyalty reinforces the Service-Dominant Logic (Vargo & Lusch, 2004), where value is co-created through reciprocal interactions between firms and consumers.

This supports the theoretical assumption that Tribe Marketing influences Customer Loyalty indirectly through psychological engagement and collaborative behavior, consistent with the Service-Dominant Logic perspective (Vargo & Lusch, 2004).

This sequential pathway supports the logic proposed in Service-Dominant Logic (Vargo & Lusch, 2004) and Tribal Marketing Theory (Cova & Cova, 2002), where value and loyalty are co-produced through social relationships rather than transactional exchanges.
The concept of value co-creation (VCC) emerged as a cornerstone of modern marketing through the Service-Dominant Logic (S-D Logic) framework introduced by Vargo and Lusch (2004).

These mediation paths are consistent with relationship marketing theories (Brodie et al., 2011) and service-dominant logic (Vargo & Lusch, 2004), which emphasize value creation as a joint process driven by social interaction and psychological involvement.
It also aligns with the Service-Dominant Logic (Vargo & Lusch, 2004), which views consumers as active partners in value creation rather than passive recipients of marketing efforts.

The significant path from Customer Engagement to Value Co-Creation reflects the principles of Service-Dominant Logic (Vargo & Lusch, 2004), which views value as being co-created through interaction and resource integration rather than unilaterally produced by firms.

Value co-creation reflects the degree to which customers and firms jointly create beneficial outcomes through participation, dialogue, and collaboration (Prahalad & Ramaswamy, 2004; Vargo & Lusch, 2004).
